title: Programme & portfolio management
blurb: Define programme and portfolio management and explain how they relate to project management.
question: Greenfield Hospital Trust is running a new patient records system, a data migration, staff training and a new car park, all at once. Its board must decide which work to fund and how to coordinate it. Which parts are a programme, which is a portfolio, and how do they relate to the individual projects?

teach.h: Zooming out from a single project
teach.body: Organisations rarely run one project at a time. Some projects are linked and only pay off together; others compete for the same money and people. So there are three levels of managing change. Project management delivers one piece of change. Programme management coordinates related pieces. Portfolio management decides which pieces the organisation should be doing at all.

Programme management is the coordinated management of projects and business-as-usual (steady-state) activities to achieve beneficial change. In plain English: running a group of RELATED projects, plus the changes to everyday working that go with them, as one coordinated effort, to deliver benefits that the projects could not achieve on their own.

Portfolio management is the selection, prioritisation and control of an organisation's projects and programmes in line with its strategic objectives and capacity to deliver. In plain English: choosing the right mix of change work, ranking it, and keeping it under review so the organisation does what best serves its strategy without taking on more than it can deliver. The items in a portfolio need not be related to each other.

teach.h: Greenfield Hospital Trust: how the levels fit together
teach.caption: The car park is unrelated to digital records, yet both sit in the same portfolio. A project can sit in a programme, or stand alone in the portfolio.

levels.label: Portfolio management
levels.sub: Selects and prioritises against strategy and capacity

levels.label: Programme management
levels.sub: Coordinates related projects and BAU for benefits

steps.label: Strategy

teach.text: Programme = RELATED projects (plus BAU) coordinated for shared benefits. Portfolio = projects and programmes that NEED NOT be related, prioritised by strategic contribution and capacity: not simply by the highest return, and not 'projects ahead of BAU'. Exam options love to swap 'related' and 'unrelated'.

rows.label: Board ranks 40 proposals and funds the top 12
Lining up the app, website and loyalty projects as one customer experience
Delivering the new booking app on time and budget
Pausing a project to free staff for a more urgent one

items: Programme management: the coordinated management of projects and BAU activities to achieve beneficial change.
Portfolio management: the selection, prioritisation and control of projects and programmes in line with strategy and capacity to deliver.
Projects deliver outputs; programmes coordinate related work for benefits; portfolios choose the right work for the strategy.
Portfolio components need not be related. A project may stand alone, sit in a programme, and sit in a portfolio.

summary: You can now define programme management (coordinating related projects and BAU to achieve beneficial change) and portfolio management (selecting, prioritising and controlling projects and programmes against strategy and capacity). You can also explain how both relate to project management, and where a single project can sit.

A.q: Complete the statement: programme management is the coordinated management of projects and ___ to achieve beneficial change.
A.why: Programme management coordinates projects AND business-as-usual (steady-state) activities to achieve beneficial change.

whyNot.0: Unrelated proposals are typical of a portfolio; a programme's work is related.
whyNot.1: Aligning work to the whole strategy is the role of portfolio management.
whyNot.3: Work packages are managed inside individual projects, not by the programme.

A.q: Which of the following best describes portfolio management?
options: Selecting and prioritising change in line with strategy
Coordinating related projects to achieve shared benefits
Managing one project's time, cost, quality and scope
Running the organisation's ongoing operations smoothly
A.why: Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls projects and programmes in line with strategic objectives and capacity.

whyNot.1: Coordinating related projects for shared benefits is programme management.
whyNot.2: Managing a single project's constraints is project management.
whyNot.3: Running ongoing operations is business as usual.

A.q: Which statement about the components of a portfolio is correct?
options: They must all share one common objective
They need not be related to each other
They must all be part of a single programme
They can only be projects, not programmes
A.why: A portfolio can hold unrelated projects and programmes; what unites them is that they are the organisation's chosen change work.

whyNot.0: Sharing one common objective is the mark of a programme, not a portfolio.
whyNot.2: A portfolio can contain several programmes and standalone projects.
whyNot.3: A portfolio contains projects AND programmes.

B.q: A city council coordinates projects to build a tram line, redesign bus routes and launch a single smartcard ticket, so that commuting becomes easier. How is this best described?
B.why: Related projects coordinated towards a shared benefit (easier commuting) form a programme.

whyNot.0: A portfolio covers all the council's change work, related or not, prioritised against strategy.
whyNot.1: There are three distinct projects here, coordinated together, not one.
whyNot.2: Building a tram line and launching a new ticket are change, not routine operations.

B.q: Which of the following is most likely to be a portfolio management decision?
options: Agreeing detailed scope for one project's next stage
Cancelling a low-priority project to fund a key one
Aligning the go-live dates of two linked projects
Updating the risk register for a single project
B.why: Choosing which work continues, and moving funding to what matters most strategically, is portfolio management.

whyNot.0: Agreeing one project's scope is project management.
whyNot.2: Aligning the timing of linked projects is programme management.
whyNot.3: A single project's risk register is managed within that project.

B.q:
Which TWO statements about programmes are correct?
1) They coordinate related projects
2) They can include BAU activities
3) Their projects need not be related
4) They select work against strategy
B.why: A programme coordinates related projects (1) and includes the BAU changes needed to realise the benefits (2).

whyNot.0: Unrelated components (3) and selecting against strategy (4) both describe portfolios.
whyNot.1: Item 3 describes a portfolio; a programme's projects are related.
whyNot.3: Item 4 describes portfolio management, not programmes.

C.q: Each quarter, a bank's change board reviews all 25 of its projects and programmes against its strategy and the staff it has available, then decides which go ahead. What is this?
C.why: Reviewing all change work against strategy and capacity and deciding what proceeds is portfolio management.

whyNot.0: Programme management coordinates a set of related projects, not the whole organisation's change work.
whyNot.1: Project management delivers a single project's objectives.
whyNot.2: Change control handles requests to change one project's baseline.

C.q: A programme includes a project to install new tills and a BAU change to how staff cash up at night. Why is the BAU change included in the programme?
options: The benefits need both new tills and new routines
BAU work must always be run as a project instead
A programme cannot contain more than one project
The portfolio has formally rejected the BAU change
C.why: Programmes coordinate projects AND business-as-usual activities, because benefits often depend on changing everyday ways of working too.

whyNot.1: BAU is not run as a project; the programme coordinates it alongside the project.
whyNot.2: Programmes typically contain several related projects.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests a rejection; the BAU change is part of the programme by design.

C.q: Which of the following statements is true?
options: Every project must sit inside a programme
A project can stand alone in a portfolio
A portfolio is a type of very large project
Programmes sit above portfolios in hierarchy
C.why: A project may stand alone, sit inside a programme, and/or sit inside a portfolio. It does not have to belong to a programme.

whyNot.0: Many projects are standalone, with no programme around them.
whyNot.2: A portfolio is a collection of projects and programmes, not a project itself.
whyNot.3: Portfolios sit above programmes, selecting and prioritising them against strategy.

reteach.title: A family moving to a new town
reteach.question: A family is relocating for a new job, and also hopes to buy a car and book a big holiday this year. Where are the projects, the programme and the portfolio?

blocks.body: Selling the old house, buying the new one and finding school places are each PROJECTS. Together, plus new everyday routines (a different school run, a new commute), they form the 'relocate the family' PROGRAMME: none of it is worth much unless it all lands together. The family's PORTFOLIO is everything they want to do this year (the move, a car, a holiday), ranked against their goals and their money and time.

blocks.text: The car and the holiday have nothing to do with the move, yet they are in the same portfolio, competing for the same budget. If money is short, the portfolio decision might be: postpone the holiday.

explain.body: A programme groups related projects and the BAU changes that go with them, and manages them together so their combined benefits are achieved. The whole is worth more than the sum of the separate projects.

test.q: Programme management aims to achieve which kind of result that separate projects could not achieve alone?
test.why: Programmes coordinate related work so that combined benefits are realised.

whyNot.0: Single outputs are what individual projects deliver.
whyNot.1: Routine efficiency is the aim of business as usual.
whyNot.3: Investment choices are made through portfolio management.

explain.h: Portfolios: the right work, at the right scale
explain.body: Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls all the organisation's projects and programmes. Two tests decide what gets in: does it contribute to the strategic objectives, and does the organisation have the capacity to deliver it?

items.label: does it help achieve the strategic objectives?
do we have the people and money to deliver it?

test.q: Portfolio management prioritises work in line with the organisation's strategic objectives and its…
test.why: Portfolios balance change against strategy and the organisation's capacity to deliver it.

whyNot.1: Share price may matter to the business, but it is not part of the definition.
whyNot.2: Supplier contracts are managed within projects through procurement.
whyNot.3: Schedules belong to individual projects, not to portfolio prioritisation.

explain.h: Each level has its own focus
explain.body: Projects focus on OUTPUTS. Programmes focus on OUTCOMES and BENEFITS from related work. Portfolios focus on STRATEGY and CAPACITY across all the organisation's change. Match the focus to the level and most questions answer themselves.

test.q: Which pairing of level and main focus is correct?
test.why: Programmes coordinate related work to deliver outcomes and benefits.

whyNot.0: Strategy is the focus of portfolio management.
whyNot.2: Outputs are the focus of individual projects.
whyNot.3: Capacity across the organisation is balanced at portfolio level.

explain.body: A project can stand alone, sit inside a programme, and/or sit inside a portfolio. A standalone project with no related work still belongs in the portfolio if it is part of the organisation's approved change.

test.q: A one-off office refurbishment is not linked to any other change, but it is on the company's list of approved change work. Where does it sit?
options: In a programme, as every project must be
Outside all governance, since it is small
In BAU, because the offices are permanent
In the portfolio, as a standalone project
test.why: Unrelated, approved projects sit in the portfolio as standalone projects; they need not belong to a programme.

whyNot.0: Projects do not have to be in a programme; this one has no related work.
whyNot.1: Small projects are still part of the organisation's governed change work.
whyNot.2: Refurbishing the offices is a one-off change, so it is a project, not BAU.
